paper.title_en: Room-Temperature Storage of Entanglement in a Silicon Carbide Quantum Node
paper.abstract_en: Robust entanglement at room temperature is a central challenge for solid-state quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced sensing. Here we demonstrate room-temperature storage of entanglement in a silicon carbide (SiC) quantum node by coherently transferring an electron-nuclear entangled state onto long-lived nuclear-spin memory qubits. Using a shallow single color center in <math display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi></mrow></math>-SiC, conventionally denoted PL6, we realize a fully addressable three-qubit register composed of one electron-spin processor and two strongly coupled <math display="inline"><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>Si</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>29</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> nuclear-spin memory qubits. This platform enables the deterministic generation of high-fidelity entangled states, including a nuclear-spin Bell state with a fidelity of <math display="inline"><mrow><mn>94</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> and a three-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ)-type state with a fidelity of <math display="inline"><mn>89</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>%</mo></math>. By implementing a swap-gate protocol in the strong hyperfine-coupling regime, the electron-nuclear entanglement is transferred to the nuclear-spin memory with a fidelity of <math display="inline"><mrow><mn>92.5</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>2.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, extending the entanglement lifetime by a factor of 240. We further confirm the generality of this approach in an additional heterogeneous <math display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>Si</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>29</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow><mtext>-</mtext><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></mrow></math> nuclear-spin register and, through a statistical survey of 200 single PL6 centers, show that multi-nuclear-spin registers occur naturally with probabilities above 10%. These results position shallow SiC color centers as a powerful platform for entanglement-assisted quantum sensing and scalable room-temperature quantum technologies.
